title: The Physics of the Burner at a Glance
lede: The burner (Aegis) runs deuterium and helium-3 in a tandem-mirror geometry, converting mostly charged products directly to electricity.
body: One reaction, one geometry, one conversion path

The burner (Aegis) is a deuterium–helium-3 (D–3He) tandem-mirror generator. Three physics choices define it: the fuel (D–3He, whose main branch releases its energy in charged particles), the confinement (an open-ended magnetic mirror plugged electrostatically at both ends), and the conversion (direct energy conversion of charged particles to DC electricity, with no steam cycle).

These choices are coupled. D–3He yields charged protons and alpha particles that an open geometry can let stream out along the field into a direct converter. That is only attractive if the neutron output stays low — here it is a 5.44% neutron fraction, which is low-neutron, not aneutronic. The operating point that makes this practical is around 90 keV ion temperature.

Everything on these pages is a design-and-simulation study. The burner is not built. Its physics carries four honest gates — end-plug coil stress, an unprecedented plug operating regime, a helium-3 supply that does not yet exist at scale, and availability short of hyperscale requirements. We state each one at full strength rather than soften it; they are physics facts, not marketing.

Read as a system, the burner is legible: a fuel chosen for charged output, a geometry chosen to let that output stream to a converter, and a conversion path chosen to skip the steam cycle. Each choice tightens the others, and each carries a named gate. The pages in this section trace those couplings from the reaction kinematics through confinement to conversion, and they end where the physics ends today — at the four gates and the test burner meant to start retiring them.
Geometry: tandem mirror, 26.49 T plug / 17 T throat
Conversion: direct energy conversion, no steam

title: The Deuterium–Helium-3 Reaction
lede: D + He-3 fuses to a helium-4 nucleus and a 14.7 MeV proton, releasing 18.35 MeV entirely in charged particles.
body: The reaction the burner is built around is D + 3He → 4He (3.6 MeV) + p (14.7 MeV). The total energy release is 18.35 MeV, and in this branch all of it appears as kinetic energy of charged particles — a helium-4 nucleus and a proton. No neutron is produced in the primary branch.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 175" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="70" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="95.0" y="100.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="95.0" y="116.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">fuel ions</text><line x1="172" y1="100" x2="215" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="217" y="45" width="180" height="110" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="307.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600"></text><text x="307" y="80" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="13" font-weight="600"><sup>4</sup>He  3.6 MeV</text><text x="307" y="112" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="13" font-weight="600">p  14.7 MeV</text><text x="307" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">18.35 MeV total, all charged</text><line x1="399" y1="100" x2="442" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="444" y="70" width="196" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="542.0" y="100.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">charged output</text><text x="542.0" y="116.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">to direct converter</text></svg>

Because the products are charged, they are steered by the magnetic field and can be collected electrostatically. That is the physical premise for direct energy conversion. In a deuterium–tritium machine, by contrast, roughly 80% of the yield is carried by a 14.1 MeV neutron, which is uncharged and must be caught in a blanket and converted as heat.
Why the charged fraction is the point

The value of D–<sup>3</sup>He is not that it is clean of neutrons — it is not — but that the dominant energy channel is charged. Charged energy can bypass a thermal cycle. The trade is a much higher required temperature and a scarce fuel; those penalties drive the burner's honest gates.

The reaction also depends on temperature: the products above are fixed by kinematics, but how often the reaction occurs is set by the ion energy and density. At the burner's ~90 keV operating point the rate is high enough to matter, though still below D–T at the same conditions. Everything downstream — direct conversion, low activation, the fuel-supply gate — follows from this one branch and the charged particles it produces.
Enables direct conversion of the main channel
Neutrons arise only from side reactions (~5.44%)

title: Why D–Helium-3 Over D–Tritium
lede: D–He-3 trades a far harder ignition condition for a mostly charged energy release and a much lower neutron flux on structures.
body: D–T is the easiest fusion fuel: its cross-section peaks near 60–70 keV and it ignites at the lowest triple product of any candidate. But four-fifths of D–T energy leaves as a 14.1 MeV neutron, activating structures and demanding a thermal blanket. The burner accepts a harder physics problem to avoid that.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="160" y="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D–T</text><text x="500" y="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D–<sup>3</sup>He</text><rect x="40" y="50" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="160.0" y="74.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">~80% energy in neutrons</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="160.0" y="124.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">peak reactivity ~64 keV</text><rect x="40" y="150" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="160.0" y="174.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">easiest to ignite</text><rect x="380" y="50" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="500.0" y="74.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">~5.44% neutron fraction</text><rect x="380" y="100" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="500.0" y="124.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">operating point ~90 keV</text><rect x="380" y="150" width="240" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="500.0" y="174.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">mostly charged output</text></svg>

The reward is physical, not economic: the main D–<sup>3</sup>He channel is charged, so it can be collected directly and the structural neutron load falls by more than an order of magnitude relative to D–T. The residual neutrons come from unavoidable D–D side reactions.

D–<sup>3</sup>He requires a higher ion temperature (~90 keV vs ~15–20 keV for D–T ignition studies), a higher triple product, and a fuel — helium-3 — that is scarce at terrestrial scale. These are exactly the levers behind the burner's honest gates, and they are the reason the breeder (Hyperion) exists: it bakes helium-3 into the program's fuel loop.

The comparison is not that one fuel is better absolutely, but that each suits a different job. D–T suits a machine whose purpose is to breed fuel and make products near-term; D–<sup>3</sup>He suits a resilient direct-conversion generator whose purpose is firm, low-activation power. The program runs both because the D–T breeder is what makes the helium-3 the D–<sup>3</sup>He burner needs — the two fuels are links in one chain, not rivals.
D–<sup>3</sup>He: hard ignition, ~5.44% neutrons, charged output
Trade favors direct conversion and low activation
Penalties: temperature, triple product, He-3 scarcity

title: The 5.44% Neutron Fraction
lede: Low-neutron is not aneutronic: about 5.44% of the burner's fusion power leaves as neutrons from D–D side reactions.
body: The burner's fusion power carries a 5.44% neutron fraction. This is low-neutron, not aneutronic. The primary D–3He branch makes no neutrons, but deuterium also reacts with deuterium, and one of those channels — plus secondary tritium burn-up — produces 2.45 MeV and 14.1 MeV neutrons. At ~90 keV with a realistic fuel mix, those side reactions leave roughly one part in eighteen of the power in neutrons.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="60" y="60" width="540" height="46" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="60" y="60" width="511" height="46" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="315" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">charged energy — 94.56%</text><text x="575" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" font-weight="600">n</text><text x="575" y="124" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">5.44%</text><text x="315" y="132" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">fraction of fusion power leaving as neutrons</text></svg>

This still matters. A 5.44% neutron fraction is low enough to make direct conversion worthwhile and to keep activation modest, but it is not zero: the first wall, plug region, and nearby structures still require neutron shielding and will see activation over their lifetime. Any claim of "clean" or "radiation-free" fusion would be false for this machine, and we do not make it.

Truly aneutronic fuels (such as p–<sup>11</sup>B) exist, but their ignition conditions are far beyond D–<sup>3</sup>He. Deuterium is in the fuel because it is abundant and its D–<sup>3</sup>He cross-section is favorable; the penalty for keeping deuterium is the D–D neutron tail.

The 5.44% is a design-point figure, not a universal constant: it moves with the fuel mix and operating temperature. What does not move is the qualitative statement — a deuterium-bearing plasma always makes some neutrons through D–D. Honest labelling matters here more than almost anywhere, because the temptation to call D–<sup>3</sup>He "aneutronic" is strong and, for this machine, wrong.
Source: D–D side reactions + secondary T burn
Shielding and activation are still required

title: The Deuterium–Deuterium Side Reactions
lede: Deuterium fusing with itself produces the burner's neutrons through two nearly equal branches, one of which breeds tritium.
body: With deuterium in the fuel, D–D fusion happens alongside the primary D–<sup>3</sup>He reaction. It splits into two branches of nearly equal probability:

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="40" y="70" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + D</text><line x1="192" y1="85" x2="235" y2="60" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="192" y1="115" x2="235" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="237" y="40" width="200" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="337.0" y="62.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600"><sup>3</sup>He + n (2.45 MeV)</text><text x="337.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">~50%</text><rect x="237" y="116" width="200" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="337.0" y="138.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">T + p</text><text x="337.0" y="154.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">~50%</text><line x1="439" y1="138" x2="482" y2="138" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="484" y="116" width="150" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="559.0" y="138.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">T burns → 14.1 MeV n</text><text x="559.0" y="154.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">secondary</text></svg>

The first branch, D + D → 3He + n, emits a 2.45 MeV neutron. The second, D + D → T + p, breeds tritium in the plasma; that tritium then burns with deuterium (D + T → 4He + n) and releases a 14.1 MeV neutron. Together these set the 5.44% neutron fraction.
Controlling the tail, not eliminating it

The neutron tail scales with the deuterium density and temperature relative to the helium-3 content. A helium-3-rich mix suppresses D–D reactions but demands more of a scarce fuel; a deuterium-rich mix eases fuel supply but raises the neutron fraction. The design point balances the two — it does not remove the neutrons, because D–D cannot be switched off while deuterium is present.

Because the tritium bred in the second branch takes time to burn, part of the neutron output is delayed relative to the primary reaction, and the balance between prompt D–D neutrons and secondary D–T neutrons shifts with confinement and temperature. Accounting for both channels, and for the tritium inventory that transiently builds in the plasma, is part of computing the 5.44% figure honestly rather than quoting only the primary branch.
D + D → T + p (~50%), then T burns → 14.1 MeV n
Tail is tunable by fuel mix, never zero with D present

title: The ~90 keV Operating Point
lede: The burner is designed to run near a 90 keV ion temperature, where the D–He-3 reactivity is high enough to be practical.
body: The burner's design ion temperature is roughly 90 keV — about 1 billion kelvin. This is far hotter than a D–T machine, which ignites in the 10–20 keV range. The reason is the D–3He cross-section: both nuclei carry a positive charge of +1 and +2, so the Coulomb barrier is higher than for D–T, and useful reactivity only builds up at tens of keV.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="170" x2="620" y2="170" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="60" y1="170" x2="60" y2="40" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M60,168 C160,160 240,120 320,95 C420,66 520,58 610,55" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="470" y1="40" x2="470" y2="170" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="470" y="32" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">~90 keV design point</text><text x="340" y="188" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">ion temperature (keV) →</text><text x="52" y="105" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">⟨σv⟩</text></svg>

Pushing higher than ~90 keV gives diminishing gains in reactivity while increasing radiation losses and confinement demands. Running much lower drops the reaction rate below what the power balance can sustain. The ~90 keV point is a compromise between reactivity, radiation losses, and what the tandem-mirror confinement can hold.

No device has sustained a D–<sup>3</sup>He plasma at this temperature and confinement in steady state. The plug operating regime required to hold such a plasma is one of the burner's honest gates: it sits well beyond the parameters any built mirror has reached.

The choice of ~90 keV is also a statement about what the confinement must deliver: hotter ions mean a higher pressure the magnetic well and plugs must hold, and a higher radiation load the power balance must overcome. The operating point is thus not just a plasma-physics number but the anchor that sets the field, the plug potential, and the engineering margins across the whole machine.
Set by the D–<sup>3</sup>He Coulomb barrier
No device has yet reached this regime steadily

title: Reactivity Versus Temperature
lede: The rate-averaged cross-section for D–He-3 rises steeply through the tens of keV and broadens past ~100 keV, framing the operating window.
body: Fusion power density scales with n<sub>1</sub> n<sub>2</sub> ⟨σv⟩, where ⟨σv⟩ is the reaction rate averaged over the ion velocity distribution. For D–<sup>3</sup>He, ⟨σv⟩ is small below 20 keV, climbs steeply through 30–80 keV, and flattens beyond ~100 keV. The burner sits on the upper shoulder of this curve near 90 keV.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="170" x2="620" y2="170" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="60" y1="170" x2="60" y2="40" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M60,169 C150,165 230,140 300,110 C380,76 470,58 610,50" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60,169 C120,150 180,80 240,64 C320,45 420,55 610,80" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/><text x="210" y="58" text-anchor="start" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">D–T</text><text x="560" y="44" text-anchor="start" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">D–<sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="340" y="188" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">temperature (keV) →</text><text x="52" y="105" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">⟨σv⟩</text></svg>

D–T (dashed) peaks near 64 keV and is larger at every temperature; D–<sup>3</sup>He (gold) peaks higher and later. The gap is why D–<sup>3</sup>He needs a higher temperature and a higher triple product to reach the same power density.

The practical window is bounded below by insufficient reaction rate and above by radiation and confinement penalties. The ~90 keV design point is chosen inside that window, accepting that D–<sup>3</sup>He will always be reactivity-limited relative to D–T.

The averaging that produces ⟨σv⟩ matters as much as the peak: because reactions are dominated by the fast tail of the distribution, the reactivity is sensitive to how well the plasma stays Maxwellian and how hot the ions run relative to the electrons. A hot-ion mode, where T<sub>i</sub> exceeds T<sub>e</sub>, both raises ⟨σv⟩ and eases the bremsstrahlung balance, which is why the burner targets it.
D–<sup>3</sup>He reactivity peaks higher and later than D–T
Operating window sits on the upper shoulder

title: The Coulomb Barrier & Cross-Sections
lede: Helium-3's double charge raises the Coulomb barrier for D–He-3, pushing the useful reaction temperature into the tens of keV.
body: Two nuclei must approach within the range of the strong force to fuse, against their mutual electrostatic repulsion. That repulsion scales with the product of the charges, Z<sub>1</sub>Z<sub>2</sub>. For D–T it is 1×1; for D–<sup>3</sup>He it is 1×2. The larger barrier means fewer ions have enough energy to tunnel through it at a given temperature.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M60,150 C260,150 300,40 340,40 C360,40 380,110 620,120" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60,150 C260,150 300,80 340,80 C360,80 380,120 620,128" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/><text x="345" y="32" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">D–<sup>3</sup>He barrier (Z=1×2)</text><text x="345" y="74" text-anchor="end" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">D–T (Z=1×1)</text><text x="340" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">internuclear separation →</text><text x="52" y="90" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">V</text></svg>

Quantum tunnelling lets fusion occur below the classical barrier height, and the reaction rate is dominated by ions in the high-energy tail of the Maxwellian distribution — the Gamow peak. Because the D–<sup>3</sup>He barrier is higher, its Gamow peak sits at higher energy, and the plasma must be hotter to populate it.

This single fact — helium-3's +2 charge — is why the burner runs near 90 keV rather than 15 keV, why its triple product target is higher, and why its confinement must be correspondingly strong. It is a fixed feature of the fuel, not a design choice that can be relaxed.

There is no way to lower the barrier — it is set by the nuclear charges — so the only levers are temperature, density, and confinement time, which is why D–<sup>3</sup>He forces a higher triple product than D–T. This is the root cause that propagates into every downstream gate: the field the plug needs, the regime it must reach, and the recirculating power the engineering gain must overcome all trace back to helium-3's +2 charge.
Higher barrier → higher Gamow peak energy
Reaction driven by the Maxwellian tail

title: Maxwellian Versus Beam-Driven Ions
lede: A thermal plasma fuses from the tail of its distribution; injected fast ions can add reactions but must be sustained against slowing-down.
body: Two ways to reach fusion energy

In a thermal (Maxwellian) plasma at ~90 keV, most ions are slower than the optimum fusion energy and the reactions come from the fast tail. An alternative is to inject energetic ions as a beam, placing population exactly where the cross-section is high. Real mirror designs use both: bulk thermal ions plus neutral-beam-injected fast ions.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 195" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="160" x2="360" y2="160" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M60,160 C120,60 160,50 210,90 C260,130 310,158 360,159" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M330,160 L330,70 L350,70 L350,160 Z" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="200" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">thermal bulk</text><text x="340" y="58" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">beam</text><text x="210" y="180" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">ion energy →</text><rect x="430" y="70" width="200" height="80" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="530.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">sloshing ions</text><text x="530.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">injected, mirror-trapped</text></svg>

Beam-driven and "sloshing" ions are central to tandem-mirror plugging: fast ions injected at an angle collect near the mirror throats, peaking the density there and building the electrostatic potential that confines the central-cell ions. But injected ions slow down by collisions and must be continuously replaced, which draws input power.

Beam sustainment always carries an efficiency penalty; too much reliance on beam-driven reactions erodes net gain. The design target is a largely thermal central cell with beams used where they do the most good — building the plug potential — rather than as the primary fusion driver.

There is also a bookkeeping subtlety: reactions between beam ions and thermal ions can dominate the fusion rate in some regimes, so the effective reactivity is not simply the thermal ⟨σv⟩. The burner design leans on beams to build the plug rather than to drive the bulk of the fusion, keeping the recirculating power within what the engineering gain can absorb.
Thermal plasma fuses from its high-energy tail
Beam/sloshing ions place population at high ⟨σv⟩
Sloshing ions build the plug potential
Beams slow down; sustaining them draws power

title: Bremsstrahlung Radiation Losses
lede: Electrons decelerating in the field of ions radiate X-rays; this bremsstrahlung is a major, unavoidable loss channel for a hot D–He-3 plasma.
body: When electrons pass near ions they decelerate and emit X-ray photons — bremsstrahlung ("braking radiation"). The radiated power scales as n<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> Z<sub>eff</sub> √T<sub>e</sub>. Helium-3 has charge 2, so a D–<sup>3</sup>He plasma radiates more bremsstrahlung than a pure hydrogenic one at the same density and temperature.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 175" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="40" y="70" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="110.0" y="100.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">hot electrons</text><text x="110.0" y="116.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">T<sub>e</sub> high</text><line x1="182" y1="100" x2="225" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="227" y="70" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="297.0" y="100.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">pass near ions</text><text x="297.0" y="116.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Z=1, 2</text><line x1="369" y1="100" x2="412" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="414" y="70" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="484.0" y="100.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">X-ray photons</text><text x="484.0" y="116.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">bremsstrahlung</text><text x="297" y="152" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12">P<sub>br</sub> ∝ n<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> Z<sub>eff</sub> √T<sub>e</sub></text></svg>

Bremsstrahlung is fundamental: it cannot be shielded or reflected back into the plasma the way some other losses can, because the plasma is transparent to hard X-rays. For D–<sup>3</sup>He, the ratio of bremsstrahlung loss to fusion power is far less favorable than for D–T, and it sets a floor on the temperature and purity the plasma must maintain to stay net-positive.

Keeping Z<sub>eff</sub> low means keeping impurities out; running at high ion temperature relative to electron temperature helps, because fusion power tracks T<sub>i</sub> while bremsstrahlung tracks T<sub>e</sub>. The burner design assumes a hot-ion mode where T<sub>i</sub> exceeds T<sub>e</sub> to keep the radiation balance workable.

Because the loss escapes the plasma entirely, it sets a hard lower bound on the fusion power density needed for net gain — the plasma must out-produce its own X-ray glow. For D–<sup>3</sup>He that bound is far closer to the achievable fusion power than it is for D–T, which is precisely why impurity control and the hot-ion mode are treated as requirements rather than refinements.
Plasma is transparent to the X-rays — they leave
Hot-ion operation (T<sub>i</sub> > T<sub>e</sub>) helps the balance

title: Synchrotron Radiation Losses
lede: Electrons spiralling in a strong magnetic field radiate at the cyclotron frequency; in the high-field plug region this cannot be ignored.
body: Electrons circle magnetic field lines and radiate at the electron cyclotron frequency and its harmonics — synchrotron (cyclotron) radiation. The radiated power scales strongly with magnetic field (roughly B<sup>2</sup>) and with electron temperature. In the burner's plug region, where the field reaches 26.49 T, this loss channel becomes significant.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="55" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M200,55 a55,55 0 0 1 40,95" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="200" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">e<sup>−</sup></text><path d="M270,90 q30,-20 60,0 M270,110 q30,-20 60,0 M270,130 q30,-20 60,0" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.3"/><text x="360" y="110" text-anchor="start" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="11">cyclotron photons</text><text x="200" y="190" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12">P<sub>syn</sub> ∝ B<sup>2</sup> T<sub>e</sub>  (partly reabsorbed)</text></svg>

Unlike bremsstrahlung, synchrotron radiation is emitted at relatively low frequencies and is partly reabsorbed by the plasma before it escapes, so the net loss depends on plasma size and opacity. In a compact, high-field region the reabsorption helps, but the raw emission is large enough that the electron temperature and field profile must be managed to keep it in check.

The plug is where the field is highest and the loss is worst, yet it is also where a strong confining potential is needed. This tension between field strength, radiation, and confinement is part of why the plug regime is one of the burner's honest gates.

The reabsorption that softens this loss depends on the plasma being optically thick at the cyclotron frequency, which in turn depends on size and density — so the same compactness that makes the plug's field so demanding also changes how much synchrotron energy escapes. Getting the field profile, temperature, and geometry to keep both bremsstrahlung and synchrotron in check simultaneously is part of what makes the plug regime narrow.
P<sub>syn</sub> rises steeply with B and T<sub>e</sub>
Worst in the 26.49 T plug region
Partly reabsorbed — net loss depends on size/opacity
Couples radiation limits to plug confinement

title: Power Balance & the Lawson Criterion
lede: Net gain requires fusion power to exceed radiation, transport, and injection losses; for D–He-3 this triple-product bar is much higher than D–T.
body: A power-producing plasma must generate more fusion energy than it loses. The bookkeeping compares fusion power against three drains: radiation (bremsstrahlung and synchrotron), transport (particles and heat leaving confinement), and the input power needed to sustain heating and plugging. Net gain requires the sum on the loss side to stay below the fusion source.
