NBI injects energetic neutral atoms that ionise and become the sloshing ions that shape the plug potential. ICRF deposits energy resonantly into the ions, supporting the hot-ion mode that keeps fusion power ahead of bremsstrahlung. ECH heats electrons locally, which is how the thermal barrier and the elevated plug potential are created and maintained.

In most machines heating and confinement are separate concerns; in a tandem mirror they are the same problem. The heating systems do not just warm the plasma — they build the very potential structure that confines it. Their power draw is therefore recirculating power that counts directly against the engineering gain.

Because the heating systems are also the confinement systems, their efficiency is a first-order term in the machine's viability rather than a secondary balance-of-plant concern. Improving injector and wave-heating efficiency directly raises the engineering gain, and any shortfall there compounds with the plug gates — which is why heating technology sits close to the centre of the burner's physics case.
NBI: creates sloshing ions, shapes potential
ECH: builds thermal barrier and plug potential

title: Fuel Mix & Neutron Yield
lede: The deuterium-to-helium-3 ratio trades neutron fraction against helium-3 demand; a He-3-rich mix runs cleaner but needs more scarce fuel.
body: The lever between neutrons and fuel

The neutron fraction is not a single fixed number of physics — it depends on the fuel mix. More deuterium relative to helium-3 raises the rate of D–D side reactions and pushes the neutron fraction up; more helium-3 suppresses D–D and lowers it, at the expense of consuming more of a fuel that is scarce at terrestrial scale. The burner's 5.44% is the design-point value for its chosen mix.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M80,60 C200,90 400,130 600,148" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><text x="120" y="55" text-anchor="start" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5">more D: higher neutron fraction</text><text x="400" y="140" text-anchor="start" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">more <sup>3</sup>He: lower, needs fuel</text><text x="330" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">He-3 fraction →</text><text x="52" y="95" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">n frac</text></svg>

This coupling ties the physics directly to the fuel-supply gate. Running cleaner (lower neutron fraction, less activation) means burning more helium-3, which worsens the ~400× supply shortfall per commercial unit. Running with more deuterium eases fuel demand but raises the neutron load on structures. There is no mix that escapes both constraints.
Why the design point sits where it does

5.44% represents a balance: low enough to keep direct conversion worthwhile and activation modest, rich enough in deuterium to keep helium-3 demand from being even more extreme. It is an honest compromise, not an optimum that removes either problem.

Because the same mix sets both the neutron load and the helium-3 draw, the design cannot minimise both at once; it can only choose a defensible point on the trade curve. The 5.44% point reflects that honesty — it is neither the cleanest nor the most fuel-frugal mix, but the balance that keeps direct conversion worthwhile without making the already-severe supply gate worse.
Neutron fraction rises with deuterium content
He-3-rich mix runs cleaner but needs more fuel
Couples directly to the He-3 supply gate

title: Ash Accumulation: Helium-4 & Protons
lede: Fusion products left in the plasma dilute the fuel and radiate; the burner must exhaust helium-4 ash and protons to sustain the burn.
body: Every D–<sup>3</sup>He reaction leaves a helium-4 nucleus and a proton in the plasma. If these fusion "ash" species build up, they dilute the fuel, raise Z<sub>eff</sub> (increasing bremsstrahlung), and eventually quench the reaction. An open-ended mirror has an advantage here: ash flows out the ends along the field with the rest of the exhaust.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="60" y="80" width="180" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">central-cell burn</text><text x="150.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><line x1="242" y1="110" x2="290" y2="110" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="292" y="80" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="367.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">products</text><text x="367.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5"><sup>4</sup>He + p</text><line x1="444" y1="110" x2="492" y2="110" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="494" y="80" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="564.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">exhausted</text><text x="564.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">out the ends</text><text x="350" y="165" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">ash removed with axial exhaust flow</text></svg>

The protons are themselves a useful product — a stream of energetic hydrogen ions — and both they and the helium-4 carry energy to the direct converter before leaving. The physics requirement is that the exhaust rate keeps the ash concentration low enough that fuel dilution and radiation stay within the power balance.

Ash exhaust competes with fuel confinement: the same end-loss channel that removes ash also removes fuel, so the plug potential and refuelling rate must be tuned to keep fuel confined while letting ash escape at a sufficient rate. This is a steady-state balance the design must maintain continuously.

An open geometry turns what is a difficult exhaust problem in a torus into a more natural one here, but it does not make it free — the exhausted ash carries fuel and energy with it, and the balance between removing ash and retaining fuel is maintained continuously by the plug potential and refuelling. Getting that steady state right is part of demonstrating a sustained burn.
Products <sup>4</sup>He and p accumulate as ash
Ash dilutes fuel and raises bremsstrahlung
Open ends exhaust ash along the field
Exhaust rate balanced against fuel confinement

title: Impurity Radiation
lede: Heavy impurities from the walls radiate strongly and raise Z_eff; keeping the plasma clean is essential to the D–He-3 power balance.
body: Why cleanliness is physics, not housekeeping

Impurities — wall-eroded metals, oxygen, carbon — are far more effective radiators than the fuel ions because radiated power scales with Z<sup>2</sup> and, for line radiation, even more steeply. A small concentration of a high-Z impurity can dominate the plasma's radiative losses and raise the effective charge Z<sub>eff</sub>, worsening bremsstrahlung across the board.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 195" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="160" x2="620" y2="160" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="100" y="130" width="40" height="30" fill="#9FB1C4"/><text x="120" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">fuel ions</text><rect x="300" y="70" width="40" height="90" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="320" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="9.5">1% high-Z</text><text x="340" y="55" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5">radiated power ∝ Z<sup>2</sup> (and more for lines)</text><text x="52" y="100" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">P<sub>rad</sub></text></svg>

For D–<sup>3</sup>He this is especially punishing because the power balance is already tight against bremsstrahlung. Even a modest impurity influx can tip the balance from net-positive to net-negative. So the first wall, plug, and expander surfaces must be chosen and conditioned to minimise erosion, and impurities that do enter must be exhausted with the ash.

Keeping Z<sub>eff</sub> near its clean value is a hard operating requirement, not a nicety. It shapes material choices, wall conditioning, and the exhaust design, and it is one reason the burner's surfaces and their maintenance receive close attention in the design.

Because the tolerance for impurities is so tight, the burner treats wall material selection, conditioning, and impurity exhaust as coupled requirements set by the power balance, not as independent engineering choices. A machine that could tolerate a dirtier plasma would have more design freedom; D–<sup>3</sup>He's radiation-limited balance removes that freedom and makes cleanliness a physics constraint.
Small impurity fractions can dominate losses
Drives material choice and wall conditioning

title: Plasma Initiation & Buildup
lede: Starting the burner means creating a target plasma, forming the mirror-trapped populations, then building the plug potential up to confining strength.
body: From vacuum to a plugged burn

Startup is a sequence, not a switch. First a low-density target plasma is created in the central cell and end regions, typically by gas breakdown and electron-cyclotron heating. Then neutral beams build the sloshing-ion and hot-electron populations at the ends. Only once those populations exist does the confining ambipolar potential begin to form.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 165" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="30" y="90" width="120" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="90.0" y="115.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">1. target</text><text x="90.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">gas + ECH</text><line x1="152" y1="115" x2="190" y2="115" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="192" y="90" width="130" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="257.0" y="115.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">2. build plug</text><text x="257.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">NBI sloshing ions</text><line x1="324" y1="115" x2="362" y2="115" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="364" y="90" width="130" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="429.0" y="115.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">3. raise φ</text><text x="429.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">potential forms</text><line x1="496" y1="115" x2="534" y2="115" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="536" y="90" width="100" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="586.0" y="115.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">4. burn</text><text x="586.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">D–<sup>3</sup>He</text></svg>

The order matters because confinement is bootstrapped: better confinement lets density and temperature rise, which raises the potential, which improves confinement further. This positive feedback is how the plasma climbs to its operating point — but it must be steered carefully, because the same feedback can stall if the plug populations are not built in the right sequence.

Reaching the ~90 keV, high-potential operating point along a stable path, without triggering the loss-cone or MHD instabilities on the way, is itself an unproven part of the physics. Demonstrating a controlled startup to a plugged D–<sup>3</sup>He burn is among the goals of the test burner.

The bootstrap is also where several gates first bite: the startup must pass through lower-potential, lower-confinement states where microinstabilities and MHD modes are most dangerous, before reaching the operating point where confinement is strong. Demonstrating a repeatable, controlled path through that valley is as much a part of proving the burner as reaching the operating point itself.
Target plasma from gas breakdown + ECH
NBI builds sloshing ions and hot electrons
Ambipolar potential forms and bootstraps τ
Stable trajectory to 90 keV is unproven

title: Honest Gate: Plug Coil Overstress
lede: At the design bore the 26.49 T plug coil is overstressed by roughly 3 to 3.9 times — infeasible as specified. This is a physics fact, stated plainly.
body: The gate, stated at full strength

The burner's end plugs require a 26.49 T field. At the design bore, the plug coil is overstressed by roughly 3 to 3.9 times what the conductor and its structure can bear as specified. In its current form the plug magnet is infeasible. We state this plainly because it is a physics-and-engineering fact, not a matter of optimism.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 195" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="160" x2="620" y2="160" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="120" y1="160" x2="120" y2="130" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="100" y="130" width="40" height="30" fill="#9FB1C4"/><text x="120" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">limit 1×</text><rect x="300" y="55" width="40" height="105" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="320" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="9.5">3×</text><rect x="420" y="40" width="40" height="120" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="440" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="9.5">3.9×</text><text x="380" y="32" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5">stress at the design bore</text><text x="52" y="100" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">coil stress</text></svg>

The cause is fundamental: magnetic pressure scales as B<sup>2</sup>, so a 26.49 T coil carries an enormous outward force that its winding and support structure must react. At the specified bore, no available conductor-and-structure combination keeps the stress within allowables by a factor of three to nearly four.
Why we do not soften it

The confining potential the burner needs requires this field; the field at this bore breaks the coil. Resolving the gap — through geometry, materials, or field-shaping — is open work, and until it closes the burner remains a design-and-simulation study. Stating the 3–3.9× overstress honestly is what makes the rest of the design trustworthy.

Nothing about the gate is hidden in an assumption: it follows directly from the specified field and bore and the strength of real conductor and structure. Closing it is legitimate future work — through field-shaping, graded coils, advanced conductors, or a revised geometry — but until a concrete design holds the stress within allowables, the honest statement is that the plug magnet, as specified, does not close.
Coil overstressed ~3–3.9× at the design bore
Cause: B<sup>2</sup> magnetic pressure on the winding

title: Honest Gate: Plug Operating Regime
lede: The plug must operate 166 to 830 times beyond any built device — a regime that cannot be post-dicted from experiment today.
body: Beyond the reach of any experiment

The end-plug plasma must operate in a parameter regime that sits 166 to 830 times beyond anything any device has achieved. Because no experiment has reached these conditions, the plug's behavior cannot be post-dicted today — there is no data to validate the models at these parameters. This is a candid statement of where the physics stands.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="90" y="135" width="30" height="15" fill="#9FB1C4"/><text x="105" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">built devices</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="560" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="6 4" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="370" y="138" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">166–830× extrapolation</text><rect x="560" y="120" width="40" height="30" fill="#D4AD5C" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><text x="580" y="170" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="9.5">plug regime</text></svg>

The plug ties together the highest field (26.49 T), a dense fast-ion population, a high confining potential, and the microstability that keeps that population intact. Every historic mirror operated far below these values. Extrapolating confinement, stability, and potential formation across two to three orders of magnitude is not something simulation alone can close credibly.

Only experiment can. A staged program — through the test burner (~2032) and beyond — would advance the achieved regime step by step, shrinking the extrapolation. Until then, any claim about plug performance at the design point is a model extrapolation, and we label it as such rather than as a demonstrated result.

The 166–830× range is not a single number because different plug parameters extrapolate by different factors; taken together they describe a regime no experiment has entered. Simulation can explore it, but simulation validated only at far lower parameters cannot be treated as prediction there — which is why the program's answer is staged experiment, and why claims about plug performance are labelled as extrapolations.
No experimental data at these parameters
Closed only by staged experiment, not simulation

title: Honest Gate: Helium-3 Supply
lede: A commercial burner unit demands roughly 400 times the domestic helium-3 supply — which is why the breeder and lunar helium-3 matter.
body: A fuel that does not yet exist at scale

Each commercial burner unit would consume roughly 400 times the entire domestic helium-3 supply. Terrestrial helium-3 exists only in tiny quantities — mostly from tritium decay in weapons stockpiles — and is spoken for by medical, security, and cryogenic uses. The burner is therefore gated on a fuel supply that does not exist at terrestrial scale.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="80" y="120" width="20" height="30" fill="#9FB1C4"/><text x="90" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">domestic supply</text><rect x="200" y="50" width="380" height="100" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><rect x="200" y="50" width="380" height="100" fill="#D4AD5C" fill-opacity="0.18"/><text x="390" y="105" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" font-weight="600">~400× per commercial unit</text><text x="390" y="180" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">annual He-3 demand vs supply</text></svg>

This single fact is why the program is built as a pair. The breeder (Hyperion) makes helium-3 as a by-product: it breeds tritium, which decays to helium-3 on a fixed physical clock, producing roughly 1.97 kg/yr of helium-3 in its design class. And over the longer term, lunar regolith holds helium-3 that could be mined. The burner cannot be fueled today from Earth's standing inventory.

The order of the program follows from this gate: build the breeder first, accumulate a helium-3 supply, and only then field burners at scale. Claiming a near-term commercial burner fleet would ignore the fuel arithmetic. The ~400× shortfall is stated exactly because it dictates the timeline.

The arithmetic is unforgiving and it drives the whole program's shape: because a single commercial unit outstrips the standing terrestrial supply by roughly 400×, there is no version of a near-term burner fleet fuelled from Earth's inventory. Stating the factor exactly is what justifies building the breeder first and treating lunar helium-3 as a serious, not decorative, part of the long-term plan.
Terrestrial He-3 is scarce and already spoken for
Breeder breeds T → He-3 (~1.97 kg/yr class)
Lunar He-3 is the longer-term supplement

title: Honest Gate: Availability Versus Tier III
lede: Modelled availability of 0.86 to 0.995 falls 30 to 100 times short of hyperscale Tier III's 0.99982 — not a sole Tier-III source today.
body: A fixed installation's power source is judged on how rarely it is unavailable. The burner's modelled availability is 0.86 to 0.995. Hyperscale Tier III data-center power is held to 0.99982. Measured by downtime, the burner as modelled is 30 to 100 times short of that standard — so it is not a sole Tier-III source today.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="90" y="90" width="60" height="60" fill="#D4AD5C" fill-opacity="0.4" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><text x="120" y="80" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5">0.86–0.995</text><text x="120" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">burner (modelled)</text><rect x="470" y="55" width="60" height="95" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="500" y="46" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5">0.99982</text><text x="500" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">Tier III</text><text x="300" y="110" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">30–100× more downtime</text></svg>

Availability is a physics-and-engineering property here, not an economic one: it reflects how often the plasma, plugs, magnets, and conversion train can be kept running without a fault-driven shutdown, and how quickly they recover. A driven plasma with an extreme plug regime has more ways to trip than a simple thermal source, and each contributes downtime.

The burner is positioned as a resilient, sovereign source that reduces dependence on the fuel-logistics tail — not as a drop-in sole source for the most demanding uptime tier. Paired with storage and other sources in a microgrid, its firmness is valuable; claiming standalone Tier-III reliability would misstate the modelled numbers.

The honest use of these numbers is comparative, not absolute: 0.86–0.995 is a respectable figure for a first-of-kind fusion source and a poor one against the single most demanding uptime tier, and both statements are true at once. Positioning the burner as a resilient, sovereign contributor within a microgrid — rather than a standalone Tier-III source — is what the modelled availability actually supports.
Not a sole Tier-III source today

title: The Honest Gates, Together
lede: Four physics gates define the burner's design stage: plug coil overstress, an unprecedented plug regime, a helium-3 shortfall, and availability short of Tier III.
body: The four gates, in one place

The burner's physics is promising and its gates are real. We state all four at full strength, because honest gates are what make the promise credible. None of them is an economic claim; each is a physics-and-engineering fact about a machine that is a design-and-simulation study, not yet built.

Two of the four — coil overstress and the plug regime — live in the end plug, the heart of the tandem mirror, and are coupled: the field that the plug needs is the field that breaks the coil, and the regime that field enables has never been tested. The other two are systemic: the fuel the machine burns does not exist at scale, and its uptime, as modelled, trails the most demanding standard.
Why they are shown, not hidden

A design that hides its gates cannot be trusted on anything else. By stating the 3–3.9×, 166–830×, ~400×, and 30–100× figures exactly, we make clear what must be solved before the burner is more than a study — and why the program builds the breeder first and stages the burner through a test machine (~2032) toward a commercial design (~2036).

Presented together, the gates also show a path: two are magnet-and-plasma problems concentrated in the end plug that a staged experimental program can attack directly, one is a fuel-supply problem the breeder is built to solve, and one is a reliability problem that improves with maturity and pairing. None is waved away, and none is presented as already solved — which is the whole point of stating them.

title: Neutron Activation & Shielding
lede: Even at 5.44%, the neutron flux activates nearby structures and demands shielding; low-neutron does not mean no shielding.
body: The consequence of not being aneutronic

The 5.44% neutron fraction is small compared with D–T's ~80%, but it is not zero. The 2.45 MeV and 14.1 MeV neutrons from the D–D side reactions penetrate matter, deposit energy as heat, and transmute nuclei in the first wall, plug region, and nearby components — leaving them radioactive. The burner therefore needs neutron shielding and manages activated material over its life.

The advantage over D–T is one of degree, and it is large: an order-of-magnitude lower neutron power means thinner shields, less activation, and lower heat-removal load on the blanket-equivalent structures. But the design still accounts for radiation damage to materials, activation of coolant and components, and the eventual handling of activated parts.

Describing the burner as "clean" or "radiation-free" would be false. It is low-neutron: meaningfully less activating than D–T, and still a nuclear machine requiring shielding, monitoring, and disciplined material management.

The activation also has a time dimension: some induced isotopes decay quickly and some slowly, so the handling and monitoring of activated material is a lifecycle concern, not a single design load. A tenfold-lower neutron source than D–T makes that lifecycle far more manageable, but it does not remove the need for shielding, monitoring, and disciplined material accounting.

title: D–T Versus D–Helium-3 Physics
lede: Side by side: the two fuels differ in ignition difficulty, neutron output, and conversion path, and each drives a different machine.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) runs D–T; the burner (Aegis) runs D–<sup>3</sup>He. The choice of fuel cascades into almost every design decision. The table below sets the physics side by side.

D–T is easier to ignite and has a larger cross-section, which is why the breeder can be the near-term machine that actually makes fuel and products. D–<sup>3</sup>He is harder in every confinement metric but offers a mostly charged output and far lower activation — the reason it is chosen for a resilient, direct-conversion generator.

The two are complementary. The breeder's D–T reaction breeds the tritium that decays into the helium-3 the burner needs. The burner's D–<sup>3</sup>He reaction delivers low-neutron, directly converted power. Neither fuel alone gives both fuel production and clean-ish direct-conversion power; together they close a loop.

The right reading of the table is that difficulty and payoff move together: D–<sup>3</sup>He asks more of confinement and fuel supply and returns a charged, directly convertible, low-activation output. Choosing it for the burner is a deliberate acceptance of the harder physics in exchange for the properties a resilient fixed-installation generator most needs.
Breeder makes the fuel the burner needs

title: Q-Engineering Versus Q-Science
lede: Scientific gain counts fusion against heating; engineering gain subtracts all recirculating power, and it is the honest test for the burner.
body: Qsci (scientific gain) is fusion power divided by the external heating power delivered to the plasma. QE (engineering gain) is net electrical output divided by total electrical input, after conversion efficiency and every recirculating draw — plug sustainment, injectors, cryogenics, and balance of plant. A machine can have Qsci above one and QE below one.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="40" y="60" width="150" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="89.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">fusion power</text><line x1="192" y1="85" x2="235" y2="85" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="237" y="60" width="120" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="297.0" y="85.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Q<sub>sci</sub></text><text x="297.0" y="101.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">÷ heating</text><rect x="40" y="140" width="150" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="169.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">net electricity</text><line x1="192" y1="165" x2="235" y2="165" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="237" y="140" width="120" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="297.0" y="165.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Q<sub>E</sub></text><text x="297.0" y="181.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">÷ all input</text><text x="430" y="90" text-anchor="start" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="11">Q<sub>sci</sub> can exceed 1</text><text x="430" y="170" text-anchor="start" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">Q<sub>E</sub> is the real test</text></svg>

For the burner this distinction is not academic. The tandem mirror spends significant power holding its end plugs — the same power that builds the confining potential. That recirculating draw sits inside Q<sub>E</sub> but not Q<sub>sci</sub>. Direct energy conversion helps Q<sub>E</sub> by converting the charged output at high efficiency, but the plug and injector power is charged against it.

We judge the burner on Q<sub>E</sub>, because that is what a power source must satisfy. The plug-regime and coil gates directly threaten Q<sub>E</sub>: if the plug cannot be sustained efficiently at the design field, the recirculating power grows and net gain shrinks. Reporting Q<sub>sci</sub> alone would flatter the machine; we do not.

Because the plug power is both what confines the plasma and what erodes the engineering gain, Q<sub>E</sub> is unusually sensitive to plug performance in a tandem mirror — more so than in machines where heating and confinement are separate. That sensitivity is why the coil-stress and plug-regime gates are not abstract concerns but direct threats to whether the burner can be a net power source at all.
Q<sub>E</sub> = net electric / total electric input
Plug + injector power sits inside Q<sub>E</sub>
Q<sub>E</sub> is the honest test for a power source

title: The Test Burner's Physics
lede: The ~2032 test burner exists to reduce the plug extrapolation with data, demonstrating startup, plugging, and direct conversion below commercial scale.
body: The burner is a design-and-simulation study today. The physics that most needs experimental data is the plug: its coil stress, its unprecedented operating regime, and the stability of its confining potential. The planned test burner (~2032) exists to move those from model extrapolation toward measurement, at a scale below the ~2036 commercial design.

A test machine cannot reach the full 166–830× regime in one jump, but it can advance the achieved parameters, validate the models that predict plug behavior, and demonstrate the operational sequence: controlled startup, sloshing-ion plug formation, a sustained ambipolar potential, a low-neutron D–<sup>3</sup>He burn, and direct energy conversion of the charged output.
What it would prove, and what it would not

Success would shrink the extrapolation and retire risk on the plug physics and conversion train. It would not, by itself, resolve the fuel-supply gate — that depends on the breeder producing helium-3 — nor guarantee Tier-III availability. The test burner is a physics milestone, honestly scoped, not a claim that the machine is finished.

Scoping the test burner honestly means being clear that it is a step, not a finish line: it narrows the plug extrapolation and demonstrates the operating sequence, and it leaves the fuel-supply and availability gates to be closed by the breeder and by fleet maturity respectively. Naming what each stage does and does not prove is how the program stays credible from design study to commercial machine.
Advances the plug regime toward the design point
Demonstrates startup, plugging, burn, and DEC
Does not by itself close the fuel or uptime gates

title: The Proton Product
lede: The 14.7 MeV proton from D–He-3 carries most of the reaction energy and, as a charged particle, is the burner's primary conversion channel.
body: The particle that carries the energy

Of the 18.35 MeV released by D + <sup>3</sup>He, the proton carries 14.7 MeV and the helium-4 nucleus 3.6 MeV — by momentum conservation the lighter proton takes the larger share. Because the proton is charged, its energy is available to direct conversion; this single particle is the main reason D–<sup>3</sup>He suits a direct-conversion machine.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="60" y="80" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="130.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="130.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">18.35 MeV</text><line x1="202" y1="95" x2="245" y2="80" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="202" y1="125" x2="245" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="247" y="55" width="170" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="332.0" y="77.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">p 14.7 MeV</text><text x="332.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">fast, charged</text><rect x="247" y="115" width="170" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="332.0" y="137.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600"><sup>4</sup>He 3.6 MeV</text><text x="332.0" y="153.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">charged</text><line x1="419" y1="77" x2="462" y2="77" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="419" y1="137" x2="462" y2="137" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="464" y="80" width="160" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="544.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">direct converter</text><text x="544.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">both collected</text></svg>

The proton's high energy is a benefit and a design constraint. It deposits some energy back into the plasma (helping sustain the burn) before it escapes, and it arrives at the direct converter as the highest-energy particle in the spectrum, setting the deepest collector voltage. Its interaction with the first wall and converter surfaces must be managed.

The contrast with D–T is stark: there, the energy leaves in a 14.1 MeV neutron that cannot be steered or collected electrically and must be caught as heat. Here, the comparable-energy particle is a proton — charged, magnetically guided, and directly convertible. That difference is the physics behind the whole burner concept.

The proton stream is also a product in its own right — a flux of energetic hydrogen ions that carries information about the burn and can, in principle, be put to use downstream. But its primary role in the physics is as the dominant charged-energy carrier, the particle that makes direct conversion of D–<sup>3</sup>He worthwhile and that fixes the top of the converter's voltage ladder.
Proton carries 14.7 MeV of the 18.35 MeV
Sets the deepest converter collector voltage
Contrast: D–T energy leaves as an uncatchable neutron

title: End-Wall Heat Flux
lede: Plasma leaving along the field concentrates enormous heat flux at the ends; the expander and converter geometry must spread it to survivable levels.
body: In a closed torus the exhaust is spread around a divertor; in an open mirror it all leaves through two ends. Without mitigation, the power streaming out of a 17 T throat would land on the end structures at a heat flux far beyond what any material survives. Managing this is a defining engineering problem of the geometry.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="110" x2="160" y2="110" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="110" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">concentrated</text><path d="M160,100 L340,50 M160,120 L340,170" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><line x1="340" y1="50" x2="340" y2="170" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="4"/><text x="340" y="190" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">spread over large end area</text><text x="250" y="55" text-anchor="start" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">expansion lowers flux</text></svg>

The remedy is the same magnetic expansion that serves conversion: fanning the field out drops the power density by the field-strength ratio, so a large end area receives a survivable flux. The direct converter is built to accept this expanded stream, absorbing charged-particle energy as collected current rather than as raw heat wherever possible.

Heat flux, direct conversion, and end-loss confinement are one linked design: the expansion needed to protect the walls is also what makes conversion and electron confinement work. Getting the geometry right at reactor power is demanding engineering, though — unlike the plug — not an open physics gate.

The reassuring part of this problem is that it is engineering, not open physics: the magnetic expansion that solves it is well understood, and the loads, while severe, are quantifiable and can be designed against with material and geometry choices. Unlike the plug gates, the end-wall heat flux does not depend on an unmeasured regime — it depends on getting a known geometry built at scale.
All exhaust leaves through two ends
Raw flux from the throat is unsurvivable
Coupled to conversion and electron confinement
